extracted.intended_audience: state permitting authorities, EPA staff, regulated entities (EGU owners/operators), and public stakeholders (permit applicants and commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on New Source Review (NSR) control-technology determinations (BACT and LAER), public participation and environmental justice considerations in permitting, Title V permit incorporation, and how to prepare and present regulatory impact analyses (RIAs) including monetized benefits (SC-GHG) and economy-wide modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancing public participation and environmental justice in permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide opportunities to enhance environmental justice by facilitating increased public participation in the formal permit consideration process (e.g., by granting requests to extend public comment periods, holding multiple public meetings, or providing translation services at hearings in areas with limited English proficiency). The permitting authority can also take informal steps to enhance participation earlier in the process, such as inviting community groups to meet with the permitting authority and express their concerns before a draft permit is issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include extending comment periods, holding multiple public meetings, providing translation services, and proactively inviting community groups to engage before draft permits are issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of public hearing under PSD regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA 165(a)(2) and 40 CFR 51.166(q)(2)(v), provide opportunity for a public hearing for interested persons to appear and submit written or oral comments on the air quality impact of the source, alternatives to it, the control technology required, and other appropriate considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure hearings and materials address air quality impacts, alternatives, control technologies, and other considerations; make clear these topics are within the hearing scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of siting, need, and environmental justice via 'alternatives' and 'other appropriate considerations'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'alternatives' and 'other appropriate considerations' language in CAA 165(a)(2) can be interpreted to provide the permitting authority with discretion to incorporate siting and environmental justice considerations when issuing PSD permits—specifically, to impose permit conditions on the basis of environmental justice considerations raised in public comments regarding the air quality impacts of a proposed source. The EAB has recognized that consideration of the need for a facility is within the scope of CAA 165(a)(2) when a commenter raises the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities may consider siting and facility need where raised by commenters and may impose permit conditions on that basis; document and explain decisions to exercise or not exercise such discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: NNSR requirement for analysis of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal regulations for NNSR permits also have an analysis of alternatives required by CAA 173(a)(5) (40 CFR 51.165(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When processing NNSR permits, include an alternatives analysis consistent with the cited statutory/regulatory requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT as case-by-case emission limitation for PSD
rubrics_metrics.description: For PSD permits, the permitting authority must establish emission limitations based on BACT for each pollutant that is subject to PSD at the new major stationary source or at each emissions unit involved in the major modification. BACT is assessed on a case-by-case basis, and the permitting authority, in its analysis of BACT for each pollutant, evaluates the emission reductions that each available emissions-reducing technology or technique would achieve, as well as the energy, environmental, economic, and other costs associated with each technology or technique. The CAA also specifies that BACT cannot be less stringent than any applicable standard of performance under the NSPS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BACT analyses must consider both effectiveness and associated energy/environmental/economic costs and be at least as stringent as applicable NSPS; document pollutant-specific determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA five-step 'top-down' BACT approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In conducting a BACT analysis, many permitting authorities apply the EPA's five-step 'top-down' approach: identify all available control options with practical application potential; evaluate and eliminate technically infeasible options; rank remaining options from most to least effective; evaluate energy, environmental, economic impacts, and other costs and eliminate options not achievable based on those considerations from the top down; select the most effective remaining option as BACT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the five-step sequence, explicitly document elimination and ranking decisions, and include analyses of technical feasibility and cost/impact tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of options that would 'redefine the source' in BACT
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of available control options need not necessarily include inherently lower polluting processes that would fundamentally redefine the nature of the source proposed by the permit applicant. BACT should generally not be applied to regulate the permit applicant's purpose or objective for the proposed facility. However, permitting authorities have discretion to conduct a broader BACT analysis if desired. The 'redefining the source' issue is ultimately a question of degree that is within the discretion of the permitting authority, and any decision to exclude an option on 'redefining the source' grounds should be explained and documented in the permit record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If excluding options because they would redefine the source, provide explanations and supporting documentation in the permit record; consider broader options only with clear justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of collateral environmental impacts in BACT
rubrics_metrics.description: In conducting the analysis of energy, environmental and economic impacts arising from each control option, permitting authorities have considerable discretion in deciding the specific form of the BACT analysis and the weight to be given to the particular impacts. Permitting authorities may consider a wide variety of environmental impacts (e.g., solid or hazardous waste generation, discharges of polluted water from a control device, visibility impacts, demand on local water resources, emissions of other pollutants subject to NSR or pollutants not regulated under NSR such as air toxics). A permitting authority could place more weight on the collateral environmental effect of a control alternative on local communities—e.g., if emission increases of co-pollutants from operating the control device may disproportionately affect a minority or low-income population—which may result in the permitting authority eliminating that control option and ultimately selecting a less stringent control technology for the target pollutant as BACT because it has more acceptable collateral impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly evaluate collateral impacts (including disproportionate impacts on EJ populations) and document how such considerations influenced elimination or selection of control options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of offsite or lifecycle impacts in BACT
rubrics_metrics.description: This analysis may extend to considering reduced, or excessive, energy or environmental impacts of the control alternative at an offsite location that is in support of the operation of the facility obtaining the permit. Example: weighing favorably a control option that involves co-firing with hydrogen produced from low-GHG emitting processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, include offsite/lifecycle environmental impacts (e.g., fuel production emissions) in the evaluation and explain how these influenced BACT selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAER definition and limits on consideration of cost and other factors
rubrics_metrics.description: For NNSR permits, LAER is defined as the most stringent emission limitation required under a SIP or achieved in practice for a class or category of sources. Unlike BACT, the LAER requirement does not consider economic, energy, or other environmental factors, except that LAER is not considered achievable if the cost of control is so great that a major new stationary source could not be built or operated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining LAER, focus on SIP or achieved-in-practice limits; do not weigh economic/energy/environmental factors except in extreme cases of prohibitively high cost that preclude source construction/operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAER cannot be less stringent than applicable NSPS
rubrics_metrics.description: As with BACT determinations, a determination of LAER cannot be less stringent than any applicable NSPS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure LAER decisions meet or exceed NSPS stringency for the pollutant/source category.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSPS as minimum baseline for BACT but BACT remains source-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: As GHGs are regulated pollutants under the PSD program, this NSPS serves as the minimum level of control in determining BACT for any new major stationary source or major modification that meets the applicability of this NSPS and commences construction on its affected EGU(s) after the date of publication of the proposed NSPS in the Federal Register. However, the fact that a minimum control requirement for BACT is established by an applicable NSPS does not mean that a permitting authority cannot select a more stringent control level for the PSD permit or consider control technologies for BACT beyond those that were considered in developing the NSPS. The authority for BACT is separate from that of BSER, and it requires a case-by-case review of a specific stationary source at the time its owner or operator applies for a PSD permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat NSPS as a floor; perform up-to-date, source-specific BACT analyses that may consider technological advances, cost changes, and other new information since the NSPS was developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSR implications of state emission guidelines and state plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Each state will develop a plan that establishes standards of performance for each affected EGU in the state that meets the applicability criteria of this emission guideline. When a stationary source undertakes a physical or operational change, even if to comply with a national or state requirement, the source may need to obtain a preconstruction NSR permit, with the type (NNSR, PSD, or minor NSR) depending on the amount of emissions increase and the area's air quality designation. However, a NSR permit may not be needed if the change will not increase emissions at the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States and sources should analyze whether required physical/operational changes will increase emissions and thereby trigger NSR; document determinations and supporting analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to conduct control-technology review if state-plan compliance triggers major NSR
rubrics_metrics.description: If a source complying with its state plan's standards of performance triggers major NSR requirements for one or more pollutants as a result of complying with its standards, the permitting authority would conduct a control technology review (i.e., BACT or LAER, as appropriate) for each of the pollutants and require that the source comply with the other applicable major NSR requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If state-plan compliance causes emission increases that meet major-source thresholds, ensure timely NSR permitting and pollutant-specific control-technology reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: State use of enforceable limits to avoid triggering major NSR (synthetic minor)
rubrics_metrics.description: States may establish enforceable conditions for a source expected to trigger major NSR that would effectively limit the unit's ability to increase its emissions in amounts that would trigger major NSR (effectively establishing a synthetic minor limitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States can design enforceable restrictions into plans to limit emissions and avoid major NSR triggers, but must ensure enforceability and proper documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title V permit requirements and schedule for incorporating newly applicable requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Title V regulations require each permit to include emission limitations and standards, including operational requirements and limitations that assure compliance with all applicable requirements. If the permit has a remaining life of 3 years or more, a permit reopening to incorporate the newly applicable requirement shall be completed no later than 18 months after promulgation of the applicable requirement. If the permit has a remaining life of less than 3 years, the newly applicable requirement must be incorporated at permit renewal. Proceedings to reopen and issue a permit shall follow the same procedures that apply to initial permit issuance and only affect the parts of the permit for which cause to reopen exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Title V schedules for reopener timing and use standard issuance procedures; limit reopenings to provisions for which cause exists and act expeditiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling state-only or not-federally-enforceable limits to support public participation in state plans
rubrics_metrics.description: If a state needs to include provisions related to the state plan in a source's title V permit before submitting the plan to the EPA, these limits should be labeled as 'state-only' or 'not federally enforceable' until the EPA has approved the state plan. The intention is to ensure that meaningful public participation is available during the development of a state plan, rather than limiting engagement to the permitting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'state-only' labels where appropriate and ensure public can comment on the plan as a whole prior to finalization; do not use permit-only mechanisms to circumvent broader plan-level public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIA separate from BSER; use of EO 12866/OMB A-4 and EPA economic guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with E.O. 12866 and 13563, the guidelines of OMB Circular A-4 and the EPA's Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses, the EPA prepared an RIA for these final actions. The RIA is separate from the EPA's statutory BSER determinations and did not influence the EPA's choice of BSER for any of the regulated source categories or subcategories. The RIA presents the expected economic consequences, including benefits and costs for illustrative scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare RIAs following EO12866/OMB A-4 and EPA guidance; present scenarios and benefits/costs transparently and maintain separation from statutory technology determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and reporting metrics in RIA (PV, EAV, snapshot years, scenario comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA evaluates impacts using the present value (PV) of costs, benefits, and net benefits for the years 2024 to 2047 from the perspective of 2019, and presents equivalent annual value (EAV). It also provides snapshot year assessments (2028, 2030, 2035, 2040, 2045) and analyzes economic/energy, environmental justice, and employment impacts across illustrative scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report PV and EAV using multiple discount rates, include snapshot years, and present scenario comparisons and supplemental analyses (EJ, employment, energy impacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple discount rates and sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA estimates PV and EAV using discount rates of 2 percent, 3 percent, and 7 percent. Specific PV/EAV results are presented at each discount rate for compliance costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide results across a range of discount rates and explain how discounting affects PV/EAV outcomes; include sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of CGE modeling (SAGE) in regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA developed a CGE model called SAGE to evaluate potential economy-wide impacts. A peer review concluded in 2020. SAGE does not currently estimate changes in emissions nor account for environmental benefits. The annualized social cost estimated in SAGE for the finalized rules is approximately $1.32 billion (2019 dollars) between 2024 and 2047 using a 4.5 percent discount rate that is consistent with the internal discount rate in the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using CGE models, disclose model capabilities and limits (e.g., SAGE does not estimate emissions/benefits), internal discounting assumptions, and interpret results in context of those limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment impact analysis in RIA
rubrics_metrics.description: An employment impact analysis describes the characteristics of groups of workers potentially affected by a regulation, as well as labor market conditions in affected occupations, industries, and geographic areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include employment impact analyses describing worker characteristics, affected occupations/industries/regions, and likely labor-market adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases (SC-GHG) and peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA analyzes climate benefits using estimates of the social cost of greenhouse gases (SC-CO2, SC-CH4, SC-N2O), reflecting recent advances and recommendations from the National Academies and the Interagency Working Group (IWG). The EPA participated in updating SC-GHG estimates, solicited comment, and conducted external peer review of technical reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use updated, peer-reviewed SC-GHG estimates where practicable, document methodological choices, and acknowledge limitations and omitted impacts in monetized estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health benefits estimation methodology (PM2.5 and ozone)
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA estimates the health benefits of changes in PM2.5 and ozone concentrations. The health effect endpoints, effect estimates, benefit unit-values, and how they were selected are described in the 'Estimating PM2.5- and Ozone-Attributable Health Benefits' TSD. Approach for updating endpoints and identifying suitable epidemiologic studies, baseline incidence rates, demographics, and valuation is summarized in the RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow documented TSD methods for endpoints, studies, baseline rates, demographics, and valuation when estimating health benefits and include references to supporting technical documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure that monetized benefits are distinct from statutory BSER determinations and have uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: The monetized benefits analysis is entirely distinct from the statutory BSER determinations and is presented solely for purposes of complying with E.O. 12866. The EPA recognizes substantial uncertainties and limitations in monetizing benefits, including benefits not quantified or monetized. The RIA emphasizes these uncertainties and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting monetized benefits, explicitly state they do not determine statutory standards, disclose uncertainties, omitted impacts, and sensitivity of results to key assumptions.
